description: Wise Tortoise is a two-person team working on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge.
summary:
This web app shows how long a lunar lander will have sunlight and contact with Earth.

You select a landing site, a landing date and a mission length. The app shows when the Sun sets, when Earth goes below the horizon, and the longest time without sunlight or contact. It also shows the best landing dates for the next 12 months.

At the south pole, the Sun and Earth stay near the horizon. Hills and crater rims can block them for many days. The app uses NASA JPL Horizons data for the positions of the Sun and Earth. It uses NASA LRO LOLA elevation data for the terrain around each site.
details:
What it does

- You select a landing site, a landing date and a mission length. You can select one of 29 sites, click a point on the south pole map, or type coordinates.

- The app shows:

- A short summary with ratings for power and communication (Good, Fair or Poor).

- The time until sunset and the time until Earth goes below the horizon.

- The percentage of the mission with sunlight, with contact with Earth, and with both.

- The longest time without sunlight and the longest time without contact.

- A timeline of the full mission.

- Terrain shadows that move with time, on a map and in 3D.

- The best landing dates for the next 12 months.

How it works

- NASA JPL Horizons gives the positions of the Sun and Earth every 30 minutes from 2026 to 2030.

- For each site, the app calculates the horizon from NASA LRO LOLA elevation maps. It uses 720 directions, up to 300 km from a lander that is 2 m tall.

- The lander has sunlight when the center of the Sun is above the horizon. It has contact with Earth when the center of Earth is above the horizon.

How we checked it

- The Sun and Earth directions agree with JPL Horizons to within 0.006° in 250 tests.

- The floor of Shackleton crater gets 0% sunlight. This is correct for a crater in permanent shadow.

- The average sunlight on the rim of Shackleton crater is 80.0%. A published study (Gläser et al. 2018) gives 81.0%.

- 56 automated tests check the calculations, the terrain and the API.

Why it is important

- Launch dates often change. At the south pole, a delay of a few days can change the sunlight and contact time by a large amount.

- The app gives this data in seconds. Students and the public can also use it to learn why the south pole is difficult.

Tools

- Python (FastAPI, NumPy) and TypeScript (Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, Observable Plot, three.js). The app runs on Vercel.

- Claude (Anthropic) wrote most of the code. Refer to AI_USE.md in the repository: https://github.com/Cp557/lunar-landing
